rows.reference: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 95.51 to 95.53 ('membra sumus corporis magni' at the end of 95.51; 'miserius est nocere quam laedi' in 95.52); same numbering in Gummere (Loeb) and Reynolds (OCT)
rows.original: membra sumus corporis magni ... miserius est nocere quam laedi
rows.translation: Latin on Perseus; R. M. Gummere (1925)
rows.says: All that is divine and human is one, and we are limbs of one great body. Nature made us kin, gave us love for one another and made us social. By her law it is more wretched to harm than to be harmed, and by her command our hands should be ready to help.
rows.bearing: Rule 7: a wider duty not to harm, grounded in the kinship of every human being, so it reaches everyone K1 and K0 protect (strangers, slaves, wrongdoers). Whoever keeps it does not kill except, at most, in defence. Counts for K1 and K0 at Clear teaching (wider rule), as in Article I row 8b. rows.says: To show that punishment should come from reason, not anger, Seneca lists things we do calmly: we kill mad dogs, slaughter savage oxen and diseased sheep so they do not infect the flock, destroy monstrous births, and drown even our own children if they are born weak or deformed. support.reconciliation:
Standing of authorities. Stoicism has no branches, no closed canon and no living authority (sources/corpus.md). Tier 1 is the surviving ethical works of Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius; Musonius Rufus, the early Stoa in later reports, Hierocles and Cicero are Tier 2 and do not count on their own; modern Stoic writers and groups are not authorities under corpus.md. So differences are between ancient teachers, and nothing above them decides.

How the school reconciles its texts. (1) The ground of the prohibition is the kinship of all human beings: we are limbs of one body and it is more wretched to harm than to be harmed (Seneca, Letter 95.51 to 95.53, counted, verified); acting against one another is contrary to nature, even towards wrongdoers (Meditations 2.1, counted, verified); and, unverified, every human being is 'a sacred thing' to others (Letter 95.33) and a fellow citizen of the larger city whom we must spare (De Ira 2.31.7). On this ground Seneca condemns a master's killing of slaves whatever the law allows (De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40) and a father's lethal cruelty to a son (De Clementia 1.15.1), all counted and verified. (2) Killing by public authority is accepted but regulated: without anger, as a last remedy for the incurable, for prevention not retribution (De Ira 1.6, 1.16, 1.19; unverified). This is context only (rule 5). (3) Revenge: Seneca's De Ira as a whole, Marcus 6.6 and 7.22 (unverified) and Musonius, Lecture 10 (Tier 2, unverified) reject retaliation and hatred; Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 (Tier 2, flagged, unverified) allows harm when provoked; De Ira 1.12 (unverified) allows defence of one's father and his 'vindication', a disputed word. (4) Newborns: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (counted, verified in an earlier session) classes drowning weak or deformed newborns as reason, not anger. The only opposing Stoic voice found is Musonius Rufus, Lecture 15 (Tier 2, unverified), who argues that every child born should be raised. No counted text narrows De Ira 1.15.2, and no authority exists to decide between Seneca and Musonius. Whether Seneca's own principle that every human being is sacred to others implies that newborns are protected, and whether Stoic doctrine treated a newborn as fully a 'homo' in the relevant sense, are Logical questions for the Register, not evidence that removes the passage. (5) War: Seneca condemns the slaughter of peoples as a 'glorious crime' (Letter 95.30 to 95.31, unverified), Marcus likens conquest to robbery (10.10, unverified), and Cicero regulates war and protects those who surrender (De Officiis 1.34 to 1.35, Tier 2, unverified); all context only.

K1.label: Contradicted
K1.reason: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (Tier 1; Stoicism has no branches, so rule 2 applies, not rule 3; content verified by search in an earlier project session, chapter not confirmed) classes drowning weak or deformed newborns as an act of reason. Under rule 9 newborns are persons, and the text approves the killing rather than reporting it (rule 4 does not apply); it is a household act, not a court or war (rule 5). For everyone else K1 is taught by verified counted wider rules (Letter 95.51 to 95.53; Meditations 2.1, reaching wrongdoers) and by verified Clear teaching for slaves (De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40) and sons (De Clementia 1.15.1). An Unclear label (rule 6) could be argued only if reviewers read the sentence as an analogy rather than Seneca's own judgement, or 'portentous births' as public religious disposal; no counted text narrows it. Musonius, Lecture 15 (Tier 2, unverified) dissents but cannot change the label (rule 1).

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Verified counted wider rules reach everyone (Letter 95.51 to 95.53, Clear teaching; Meditations 2.1, which forbids anger and hatred towards wrongdoers), and verified Clear teaching condemns a master's killing of a slave in anger (De Ira 3.40) and in cruelty (De Clementia 1.18). De Ira 1.15.2 is expressly 'not anger', so it does not contradict K0's anger clause. Caveats: if 'separating the useless from the sound' is read as killing for one's own gain, K0 would become Unclear (rule 6); De Ira 1.12 ('vindicabit', 'exsequar') could bear on the revenge clause but is unverified and its key word is disputed. Unverified Explicit support (De Ira 1.5.2; Letter 95.30 to 95.33; De Ira 2.31.7) would strengthen this once checked.

K3.label: Silent (on verified evidence)
K3.reason: No verified counted text addresses non-combatants in war. Letter 95.30 to 95.31 (Tier 1, unverified) condemns killing in war as such, a wider rule that would make K3 Taught (wider rule) once verified; Meditations 10.10 (unverified) is Implied only; Cicero, De Officiis 1.34 to 1.35 (Tier 2, flagged, unverified) protects those who surrender but is not counted. K3 is a record wording and is context only (rule 5).

rows.reference: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (modern Loeb and Latin Library numbering; Stewart divides chapters differently, and the chapter number was not confirmed by search)
rows.original: liberos quoque, si debiles monstrosique editi sunt, mergimus; nec ira sed ratio est a sanis inutilia secernere
rows.translation: Aubrey Stewart (1889); Latin as in the standard text (the Latin itself was not shown by any search)
rows.says: Seneca argues that punishment should come from reason, not anger, and lists things 'we' do calmly: we kill mad dogs and savage oxen, put sick sheep to the knife so they do not infect the flock, destroy monstrous births, and drown our children too if they are born weak or deformed. It is not anger but reason, he says, to separate the useless from the sound.
rows.bearing: K1: Contradicted (rules 2, 5 and 9). Newborns are persons for K1 (rule 9). The drowning is done by the parents on their own authority, not by a court or ruler, so exclusion (a) does not cover it (rule 5). Seneca does more than report a custom: he calls the act reason, which in Stoic terms is right action, so rule 4 does not apply. Stoicism has no branches, so this is rule 2, not rule 3. Narrower reading considered: 'portentosos fetus' may mean prodigies that public religious authority ordered destroyed, but 'debiles' (weak) reaches beyond prodigies, so the clause on children most naturally means a private practice (this point rests on general knowledge, not on a verified source). Roman law may also have allowed or required killing a markedly deformed infant (Cicero, De Legibus 3.19, citing the Twelve Tables; outside the corpus, unverified); a law that lets a father kill is still not a court's or ruler's sentence (rule 5). K0: not contradicted, because the passage expressly denies that anger is the motive; whether getting rid of 'the useless' counts as killing 'for your own gain' is a hard case (rule 6) left open. K3: no bearing. Note that the same passage supports K0's anger clause: even killings Seneca accepts must not be done in anger.
rows.strength: n/a (counter; Seneca's approval is stated, 'nec ira sed ratio est')

counter.reconciliation:
Stoicism has no branches, no closed canon, no council and no living authority (sources/corpus.md, section 8). Modern Stoic writers and groups are not authorities. So any reconciliation is between ancient teachers, and a Tier 2 or later voice cannot outweigh a counted text (METHOD.md section 9, decision 7).

(1) Newborns. Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (Tier 1, verified by search in an earlier session) calls drowning weak or deformed newborns an act of reason. The only direct Stoic opposition found is Musonius Rufus, Lecture 15 (Tier 2, not counted, unverified): every child born should be raised, and getting rid of later children to enrich earlier ones is impious. Epictetus, Discourses 1.23 (Tier 1, unverified) defends natural love of offspring against Epicurus but does not address weak or deformed infants. Seneca's own universal teaching (Letter 95.51 to 95.53, Tier 1, verified; De Ira 2.31.7, Tier 1, unverified) makes every human being a limb of one body, but no Stoic text applies it to withdraw 1.15.2. The early Stoic view that the soul arises at birth and reason comes later (Plutarch and Aetius, outside the corpus) may explain Seneca's classification, but rule 9 sets it aside. Within the tradition this is an unresolved disagreement between Seneca (counted) and Musonius (not counted), and on the counted texts Seneca's passage stands.

(2) Children and slaves beyond infancy. Counted texts condemn lethal cruelty by those in charge of a household: a father who flogged his son to death (De Clementia 1.15.1), and masters who kill slaves or feed them to lampreys (De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40). Seneca limits a Roman law that let masters do almost anything to slaves by appeal to the shared law of living beings. He does not reject masters' power, and non-lethal punishment, even breaking a slave's legs, remains within it (De Ira 3.32). A father's family court is presupposed but praised only for mercy (Tarius, De Clementia 1.15.2 to 1.15.7).

(3) Anger and revenge. De Ira as a whole, with Meditations 2.1 and 6.6 (Tier 1, verified), Epictetus, Discourses 1.18 and 1.28 (Tier 1, unverified) and Musonius, Lecture 10 (Tier 2, unverified), teaches that no harm, punishment included, should be done from anger, and that revenge is not to be sought. Against this, Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 (Tier 2, flagged, verified) allows harm in return for wrong; it is not counted. De Ira 1.12 (Tier 1, unverified) lets a son defend his father without anger and then 'pursue' (exsequar) the killing; whether that means prosecution or vengeance is open.

(4) Tyrants. Cicero, De Officiis 3.19 and 3.32 (Tier 2, flagged, unverified) calls killing a tyrant honourable. Seneca, De Beneficiis 2.20 (Tier 1, unverified) says Brutus did not act on Stoic teaching in killing Caesar. No counted text was found that approves tyrannicide.

(5) Courts and war (context only). Seneca allows lawful death sentences only as a last remedy, without anger, like a physician (De Ira 1.6, 1.16 and 1.19, unverified). He condemns killing as a spectacle (Letters 7 and 95.33, unverified) and wars of conquest (Letter 95.30 to 95.31, unverified). Marcus calls those who glory in capturing Sarmatians robbers (Meditations 10.10, unverified). Cicero (Tier 2) asks that those who surrender be received, but approves razing Carthage and Numantia.

(6) One's own death (exclusion (d), context only). The Stoics allowed a reasoned exit from life (Seneca, Letter 70; Diogenes Laertius 7.130, Tier 2). Neither permits killing another person.

K1.label: Contradicted
K1.reason: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (Tier 1; Stoicism has no branches, so rule 2 applies, not rule 3) lists drowning children born weak or deformed among acts done by reason, not anger ('nec ira sed ratio est'). That is approval of a deliberate killing of newborns by their parents on private authority, so neither rule 4 nor exclusion (a) applies (rules 2, 5 and 9). No counted text removes it: Epictetus 1.23 (unverified) speaks only of natural love of offspring, and the one direct Stoic opposition, Musonius Rufus, Lecture 15, is Tier 2 and unverified (rule 1). For everyone beyond infancy, verified counted texts protect children, slaves and all people (De Clementia 1.15.1 and 1.18; De Ira 3.40; Letter 95.51 to 95.53). Caveats: the deciding row was verified by search in an earlier session and not re-checked in this run; the chapter number rests on modern numbering; the Latin was not shown by search. If the project lead read the passage as an argument by analogy that only presupposes a Roman custom (rule 4), the label would fall to Unclear (rule 6), but the earlier independent verifier judged it an endorsement, and the households annex (ST-11) reads it the same way.

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Verified counted texts teach that no harm, punishment included, may be done from anger or for revenge, and condemn killings by fathers and masters done in anger or cruelty: De Ira 1.15 (even acceptable killings must come from reason, not anger), De Ira 3.32 (wait until anger has passed), De Ira 3.40 and De Clementia 1.18 (masters who kill slaves condemned), De Clementia 1.15.1 (a father who flogged his son to death condemned), Meditations 2.1 (no anger at or hatred of wrongdoers) and 6.6 (the best revenge is not to become like the wrongdoer). Letter 95.51 to 95.53 gives a wider duty not to harm that reaches every human being (rule 7). No counted text approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. Hard cases: De Ira 1.15.2 is expressly not from anger, and whether ridding oneself of 'the useless' counts as killing 'for your own gain' is unresolved (rule 6); De Ira 1.12's 'exsequar' (avenge or prosecute) is unverified; Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 (harm in return for wrong) is Tier 2 and does not count. If the 'own gain' reading of De Ira 1.15.2 were adopted, the label would be Unclear.

K3.label: Silent (provisional)
K3.reason: No verified counted text speaks either way about killing non-combatants in war. Unverified Tier 1 leads point towards taught in part: Letter 95.30 to 95.31 condemns wars of conquest and the slaughter of whole peoples without naming non-combatants; De Clementia 1.18.1 says nature bids us spare even captives (phrase not confirmed by search, and its context is slaves); Meditations 10.10 calls those who glory in capturing Sarmatians robbers. Cicero, De Officiis 1.34 to 1.35 (Tier 2, not counted, unverified) requires receiving those who surrender but approves razing Carthage and Numantia. War is context only (rule 5); none of these decides a label until verified.

rows.original: liberos quoque, si debiles monstrosique editi sunt, mergimus; nec ira sed ratio est a sanis inutilia secernere (standard Latin text; never displayed by any search in any session)
rows.says: Arguing that punishment should come from reason, not anger, Seneca lists things 'we' do calmly: we kill mad dogs, slaughter a fierce ox, put diseased sheep to the knife so they do not infect the flock, destroy monstrous offspring (portentosos fetus: in a list of animals this may include animal births or public prodigies), and drown our children too if they are born weak and deformed. It is not anger but reason, he says, to separate the useless from the sound.
rows.bearing: K1: Contradicted (rules 2, 5 and 9). Newborns are persons for K1 (rule 9). The decisive clause is 'liberos quoque ... mergimus' (our children too we drown): an act of parents and households, not of a court or ruler, so exclusion (a) does not cover it (rule 5); a Roman law letting or telling a father do it would still not be a court's sentence. Seneca does more than report a custom: 'nec ira sed ratio est' classes it as reason, and he uses it as a model for right punishment, so rule 4 does not apply. No branches, so rule 2, not rule 3. Points reviewers may weigh: (i) the sentence is a premise in an argument about anger; (ii) modern scholars connect drowning with the public expiation of prodigies (outside the corpus, see the Roman law context row). Neither is a narrowing reading by the tradition's own counted texts, commentators or authority, so rule 6 does not apply as written. K0: hard case (rule 6): the stated motive is not anger, hatred or revenge, but whether ridding the household of a child it judges 'useless' is killing 'for your own gain' is unresolved. The same passage supports K0's anger clause.

verified.reconciliation:
Standing of authorities. Stoicism is a closed ancient school with no branches, no commentarial tradition and no living authority (sources/corpus.md). Tier 1 is the ethical works of Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. Musonius Rufus, Hierocles, Diogenes Laertius and Cicero are Tier 2 and do not count on their own. Modern Stoic writers and groups are not authorities. So any differences are between ancient teachers, and no one stands above them to decide. No counted text or classical commentator narrows another.

(1) Why harming is wrong. The school grounds the duty not to harm in the kinship of all human beings. We are limbs of one body, and it is more wretched to harm than to be harmed (Letter 95.51 to 95.53, verified in an earlier session). Acting against one another is contrary to nature, even towards wrongdoers, whom one must not hate (Meditations 2.1, verified earlier). Unverified texts say this more strongly: every human being is 'a sacred thing' to others (Letter 95.33), and we must spare every fellow citizen of the world (De Ira 2.31.7).

(2) Power in the household. Seneca limits the power Roman law gave masters and fathers, but does not reject it. A master's cruel killing of slaves is condemned whatever the law allows (De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40). A father who flogged his son to death is held up as hated (De Clementia 1.15.1). Both were verified earlier. Harm short of death stays within a master's power, even breaking a slave's legs, and only anger and haste are faulted (De Ira 3.32). A father's household court is praised only for mercy (Tarius, De Clementia 1.15.2 to 1.15.7).

(3) Newborns. De Ira 1.15.2 (verified earlier) classes drowning weak or deformed newborns as reason, not anger. Several voices go the other way, but none can override it:
- Musonius Rufus, Lecture 15 (Tier 2; only its thesis is corroborated, by scholarly sources) says every child born should be raised.
- Hierocles (Tier 2, unverified) says the same of all or most children.
- Epictetus, Discourses 1.23 and 1.11 (Tier 1, unverified) teach natural love and care of offspring, but at the Implied level and not about weak or deformed infants.
Within the school this is an unresolved disagreement between Seneca (counted) and Musonius (not counted). No counted text narrows Seneca's sentence. Does Seneca's own principle that every human being is kin imply that newborns are protected? That is a Logical question for the Register, not a narrowing reading by the tradition. The early Stoic view that a newborn has not yet developed reason (outside the corpus) may explain Seneca's view, but rule 9 sets it aside.

(4) Anger and revenge. Verified counted texts teach that no harm, punishment included, should be done in anger (De Ira 3.32 and 3.40), and that one should not hate wrongdoers (Meditations 2.1) or take revenge in kind (Meditations 6.6, verified earlier). Unverified texts add more: Epictetus 1.18 and 1.28, Meditations 7.22, and Musonius, Lecture 10 (Tier 2). Against this, Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 (Tier 2, flagged, verified) allows harm in return for a wrong. De Ira 1.12 (unverified) lets a son defend his father without anger and then 'pursue' his killing; whether that means prosecution or vengeance is open.

(5) Tyrants. Cicero, De Officiis 3.19 and 3.32 (Tier 2, unverified) calls killing a tyrant honourable. Seneca, De Beneficiis 2.20 (unverified) faults Brutus's judgement, not tyrannicide as such. De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20 (unverified, content uncertain) may treat the death of an incurable tyrant as a benefit. No verified counted text approves tyrannicide.

(6) Context only. Seneca allows death sentences by public authority only as a last remedy and without anger (De Ira 1.6, 1.16 and 1.19, unverified). He condemns killing as a spectacle (Letters 7 and 95.33) and the slaughter of whole peoples (Letter 95.30 to 95.31), both unverified. Marcus calls glory in capturing Sarmatians robbery (10.10, unverified). Cicero (Tier 2) protects those who surrender but approves razing Carthage and Numantia. The Stoics allowed a reasoned exit from one's own life (exclusion (d)).

K1.label: Contradicted
K1.reason: Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 is a Tier 1 text, and Stoicism has no branches, so rule 2 applies, not rule 3. It says 'liberos quoque, si debiles monstrosique editi sunt, mergimus; nec ira sed ratio est'. That is approval of parents deliberately drowning newborns born weak or deformed: it is classed as reason and used as a model for right action, so rule 4 does not apply. It is done on household authority, not by a court or ruler, so rule 5 does not apply. Newborns are persons (rule 9). No counted text, classical commentator or authority narrows it, so rule 6 does not apply as written. Musonius, Lecture 15 dissents, but it is Tier 2 and unverified (rule 1). For everyone beyond infancy, verified counted texts teach K1: the wider rules in Letter 95.51 to 95.53 and Meditations 2.1 (which reach wrongdoers), and Clear teaching for slaves (De Clementia 1.18; De Ira 3.40) and sons (De Clementia 1.15.1). Caveats: (i) the deciding row rests on a search in an earlier session that I could not repeat; its chapter number and Latin were never shown by search. (ii) If the project lead reads the sentence as an analogy that only presupposes a Roman custom, or reads the drowning as public expiation of prodigies, the label would fall to Unclear (rule 6). Two earlier project checks read it as approval, and so do I. (iii) De Beneficiis 7.19 to 7.20 (unverified) may be a second, harder case about tyrants.

K0.label: Unclear
K0.reason: Verified counted texts teach each clause. Anger: De Ira 3.40 and 3.32, and Meditations 2.1. Hatred: Meditations 2.1. Revenge: Meditations 6.6. A wider duty not to harm anyone, which also reaches killing for gain: Letter 95.51 to 95.53. But De Ira 1.15.2 is a counted text approving a deliberate killing of newborns by parents. Its stated motive is 'to separate the useless from the sound', which is expressly not anger and is not hatred or revenge. Whether getting rid of a child the household judges useless counts as killing 'for your own gain' is not settled by the wording. If it does, K0 is Contradicted (rule 2); if it does not, K0 is Taught. Both researchers flagged this and labelled Taught. I label it Unclear because the label depends on this unresolved hard case (rule 6). The project lead should decide what 'for your own gain' covers and apply the same reading to every tradition. Two other texts do not decide: De Ira 1.12 ('exsequar', avenge or prosecute) is unverified, and Cicero, De Officiis 1.20 is Tier 2.

Letter 95.30 to 95.31 condemns 'the glorious crime' of slaughtering whole peoples. K3 is a record wording; war is context only (rule 5).

verified.branch_notes: Stoicism has no branches (sources/corpus.md), so each label applies to the whole tradition, and rules 2 and 7 apply rather than rules 3 or branch-limited findings. The only internal division found is between teachers. On newborns, Seneca (Tier 1, approving) and Musonius Rufus (Tier 2, opposing) disagree; Hierocles (Tier 2) probably sides with Musonius. On harm in return for a wrong, Cicero (Tier 2, non-Stoic) and Marcus Aurelius and Musonius disagree. There is no authority to settle either. Not checked: the early Stoa beyond Diogenes Laertius 7.32 to 7.33 and 7.130 (both unverified), the fragments of Zeno and Chrysippus in other ancient reports (outside the corpus), Epictetus' Fragments (Tier 2, flagged), and modern Stoic bodies, which corpus.md says are not authorities.
verified.fairness_notes:
1. No way to narrow a hard text. Traditions with classical commentators or an authorised interpreting body can have a hard text narrowed into 'Unclear' (rule 6). Stoicism is a closed ancient school with neither, so one sentence of Seneca, written as a premise in an argument about anger, decides K1 for the whole tradition. An adherent may see this as a structural disadvantage. The rule is applied the same way, but it does not bite the same way. This should be said openly in the article.
2. Where the line is drawn for Musonius. corpus.md keeps Musonius Rufus in Tier 2 only because his lectures survive in excerpts, and admits 'a fair case for Tier 1'. He is the Stoic who argues that every child should be raised. Counting him would probably not change K1, since he opposes Seneca rather than narrowing him (rule 2). But the article should say the school was divided, not present Seneca's sentence as 'the Stoic view'.
3. Same standard for approval. Seneca's 'we drown' describes Roman practice. He goes beyond reporting it, by classing it as reason and using it as a model. Other traditions' texts that describe their society's practice and call it right must get the same reading. Texts that only presuppose a practice must stay Implied for every tradition alike (rule 4).
4. Same standard for wider rules. The Stoic wider rules (Letter 95.51 to 95.53; Meditations 2.1) are credited at Clear teaching, as similar wider rules were credited for Sikhism and secular humanism in Article I.
5. Same standard for 'own gain'. K0 turns on what 'for your own gain' covers. The project must apply one reading to every tradition with an approved killing of a 'burdensome' or 'useless' person. Otherwise Stoicism could be marked Contradicted or Unclear where another tradition is let through, or the reverse.
6. Uneven verification. In this run no search was possible. The deciding counter-text (De Ira 1.15.2) was verified in an earlier session, while several of the strongest supporting texts were never verified: Letter 95.30 to 95.33 ('homo, sacra res homini'), De Ira 2.31.7 and De Ira 1.5.2 (Explicit or Clear if verified). So the support side looks thinner than the texts probably are. This does not change K1 (rule 2), but the article should not present the evidence for Stoicism as mostly negative.
7. Modern Stoics reject infanticide, but under CLAUDE.md decision 2 and corpus.md modern practice is not evidence. This is the same standard as for every other tradition.
